title: Physics Problem-Solving: A Step-by-Step Approach
metaTitle: Physics Problem-Solving: A Step-by-Step Approach | GuruForU
metaDescription: Physics problems look overwhelming until you use a repeatable process: list, diagram, equation, units, and a sanity check. A parent and student guide.
lead: Physics problems can look overwhelming: a paragraph, a diagram, three numbers, and a quantity you have never calculated before. Talent is not what separates students who finish them from students who freeze. A repeatable process is—identify what you know, what you need, and which relationship connects them. This guide turns that process into steps you can use on homework, quizzes, and exam papers from first-year physics through GCSE and high school.

sections.title: Why Physics Feels Harder Than the Formula Sheet
content: Students often think physics is 'remembering which equation.' The formula sheet is the easy part. The hard part is translating a story into symbols: which quantity is the unknown, which values are given, and which equation is even allowed. Two problems can use the same formula and look nothing alike.

The other trap is jumping to the calculator. Plugging numbers before the setup is clear produces answers with the wrong units, the wrong variable, or a sign that cannot exist. Slowing down for sixty seconds of listing and sketching is faster than restarting three times.

highlights.title: Physics is translation
highlights.text: Words and diagrams become a short list of symbols. If the list is wrong, every equation after it is theatre.

highlights.title: One process, many topics
highlights.text: Kinematics, forces, energy, and circuits all yield to the same habit: knowns, unknown, picture, equation, units, check.

highlights.title: Partial credit lives in the setup
highlights.text: Exam boards and teachers mark the method. A boxed wrong number with no working scores worse than a clear setup and an arithmetic slip.

sections.title: Step 1: Read and List
content: Read the whole problem once without writing. Then read it again and write a list. Include units. Write what you are solving for as a symbol, not as a sentence. Often the act of organising the information reveals the path forward.

list.item: Givens: m = 2.0 kg, v = 4.0 m/s, t = 3.0 s. If a value is 'at rest,' that is v = 0, not a missing number
Unknown: What is a? What is F? Name it. If the question asks for two things, list both before starting
Implied facts: g ≈ 9.8 or 10 m/s², horizontal projection, frictionless—these are givens even when no digit appears
Cross out extras: A mass that never enters the energy equation is a distractor. Listing still helps you ignore it later

sections.title: Step 2: Draw, Then Pick the Equation
content: Most problems use a handful of core relationships. Match the variables you have and need to an equation that connects them. Draw a diagram when motion or forces are involved—a blob with arrows is enough. A free-body diagram is not decoration; it is how you know whether to use F = ma, energy, or kinematics.

strategies.title: Kinematics (motion without worrying yet about why)
strategies.text: If the problem gives acceleration, time, and a velocity or displacement, the SUVAT / kinematic equations are the usual path. Sketch a timeline: start, finish, direction.

strategies.title: Forces
strategies.text: If the problem mentions push, friction, weight, or 'net force,' draw every force, choose a positive direction, then write ΣF = ma. Missing a force is the most common error—not the algebra.

strategies.title: Energy
strategies.text: If height, springs, or 'how fast at the bottom' appear, try conservation of energy before hunting for acceleration. Energy often skips the messy middle of the motion.

strategies.title: When two equations seem possible
strategies.text: Use the one that matches the givens you actually have. If you would need a quantity the problem never gave and you cannot find it, you picked the wrong tool.

sections.title: Step 3: Units Matter
content: Convert everything to a consistent system before plugging in—usually SI (metres, kilograms, seconds, newtons). Check that units cancel correctly in the final answer. Dimensional analysis catches many mistakes that a calculator will happily hide.

list.item: cm to m, g to kg, minutes to seconds: Do this on the list, not in your head mid-equation
km/h to m/s: Divide by 3.6. Mixing km/h with seconds is a classic exam trap
Write units through the algebra: If you wanted newtons and your units simplify to kg·m/s², you are on track. If they simplify to seconds, you are not

sections.title: Step 4: Check Reasonableness
content: Does the answer make sense? Negative time? A car going 500 m/s? A 2 kg book weighing 2000 N? Sanity-check your result before moving on. If it fails the smell test, the mistake is usually in the list or the diagram, not in the last line of arithmetic.

highlights.title: Order of magnitude
highlights.text: Walking speed is about 1 m/s, a car about 30 m/s, sound about 340 m/s. Answers far outside those bands for everyday objects are probably wrong.

highlights.title: Sign and direction
highlights.text: A negative velocity can be fine if you defined a direction. A negative mass or a negative time for 'how long until' is not.

highlights.title: Compare to a simpler case
highlights.text: If friction were zero, would the answer get larger or smaller? If your result went the other way, the setup is inverted.

sections.title: A Worked Pattern You Can Reuse
content: Example type: A 1.2 kg cart, initially at rest, is pushed with a net force of 3.6 N. How fast is it going after 2.0 s?

List: m = 1.2 kg, F_net = 3.6 N, v₀ = 0, t = 2.0 s, unknown = v. Diagram: arrow for force in the positive direction. Equation: a = F/m = 3.0 m/s², then v = v₀ + at = 6.0 m/s. Units: N/kg = m/s²; (m/s²)·s = m/s. Check: from rest, a gentle push for two seconds should be a jogging speed, not highway speed. Done.

sections.title: How Parents Can Help Without Solving It
content: Ask to see the list and the sketch before any calculator use. If those are empty, the issue is not 'they don't know physics'—they skipped the process. If the list is complete and the equation is still wrong, that is a teaching moment for a tutor or the teacher, not a reason to take over the algebra.

faq.question: What is the first step in solving a physics problem?
faq.answer: Read and list: write down given quantities with units and what you are solving for. Organising the information often reveals the path forward.

faq.question: How do I pick the right equation for a physics problem?
faq.answer: Match the variables you have and need to a relationship that connects them. Draw a diagram for motion or forces. If you would need a quantity the problem never gave, you likely picked the wrong tool.

faq.question: Why do units matter in physics?
faq.answer: Convert to SI (or one consistent system) before plugging in. Check that units cancel to the unit of the unknown. Dimensional analysis catches many mistakes a calculator will not.

faq.question: How do I check if my physics answer is reasonable?
faq.answer: Sanity-check before moving on. Negative time, a car at 500 m/s, or a book weighing thousands of newtons means recheck the list and diagram—not just the last calculation.

faq.question: Can a tutor help if my child understands the class but fails problems?
faq.answer: Yes. That pattern usually means the process (translation and setup) is missing, not the concept. GuruForU tutors practise that process on the student's own assignments.
